Consistency across all business operations - Future-proofing for API extraction Architectural Patterns Primary Architectural Patterns 1. Layered Architecture (N-Tier) Description: The application follows a classic 5-layer architecture with strict unidirectional dependencies flowing downward: Presentation → Business Services → Domain → Data Access → Infrastructure. Each layer has clearly defined responsibilities and communicates only with adjacent layers (except Infrastructure, which is referenced by all). Structure: ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Presentation Layer (MVC Web + Controllers) │ │ - ASP.NET MVC 2 Web Application │ │ - Controllers (HTTP request handling) │ │ - View Models │ │ - Views (ASPX templates) │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ↓ depends on ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Business Services Layer │ │ - Business workflow orchestration │ │ - Request/Response messaging │ │ - Domain event handlers │ │ - Entity to ViewModel mapping │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ↓ depends on ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Domain Model Layer (DDD) │ │ - Entities and Aggregates │ │ - Business rules and invariants │ │ - Domain events │ │ - Repository interfaces │ │ - Value objects │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ↓ depends on ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Data Access Layer (NHibernate) │ │ - Repository implementations │ │ - ORM mappings (HBM.XML) │ │ - Unit of Work implementation │ │ - Query translation │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ↓ uses ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Infrastructure Layer (Cross-Cutting Concerns) │ │ - Authentication & Authorization │ │ - Logging (Log4Net) │ │ - Configuration │ │ - Email, Payments │ │ - Domain base classes │ │ - Repository & Unit of Work abstractions │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Characteristics: - Each layer is implemented as separate Visual Studio project - Dependencies are explicit via project references - No circular dependencies detected - Infrastructure layer provides foundation abstractions (no upward dependencies) Benefits: - ✅ Excellent separation of concerns - ✅ Easy to understand for new developers - ✅ Testable (can mock dependencies between layers) - ✅ Maintainable (changes localized to specific layers) - ✅ Independent layer evolution possible Trade-offs: - ⚠️ All requests pass through all layers (potential performance overhead) - ⚠️ Can lead to anemic domain model if business logic leaks to services - ⚠️ Tight coupling within monolith (difficult to extract microservices) 2. Domain-Driven Design (DDD) Description: The application demonstrates strong DDD tactical patterns implementation with well-defined aggregates, entities, value objects, domain events, repositories, and domain services. Business logic is encapsulated within the domain model rather than scattered across services. DDD Building Blocks Implemented: Aggregate Roots: - Basket - Shopping basket aggregate root - Order - Order aggregate root - Customer - Customer aggregate root - ProductTitle - Product catalog aggregate root Entities: - BasketItem , OrderItem , Product , DeliveryAddress , Payment Value Objects: - Address - Immutable address value object - Money-related values (embedded in entities) Domain Events: - OrderSubmittedEvent - Raised when order is submitted, triggers email notification Repositories (Interfaces in Domain): - IBasketRepository , IOrderRepository , ICustomerRepository , IProductRepository Domain Services: - ShippingService - Calculates shipping costs based on delivery options Factories: - BasketItemFactory - Creates basket items with proper initialization - OrderItemFactory - Creates order items from basket items - PaymentFactory - Creates payment objects Specifications: - EmailValidationSpecification - Validates email format Example Domain Logic: // Domain entity encapsulates business rules public class Basket : AggregateRoot { public void AddItem ( Product product , int quantity ) { // Business rule: quantity must be positive if ( quantity <= 0 ) throw new DomainException ( "Quantity must be greater than zero" ); // Business rule: check if item already exists var existingItem = Items . FirstOrDefault ( i => i . ProductId == product . Id ); if ( existingItem != null ) { existingItem . IncreaseQuantity ( quantity ); } else { Items . Add ( BasketItemFactory . Create ( product , quantity )); } // Aggregate maintains own consistency RecalculateTotal (); } } Benefits: - ✅ Business logic clearly encapsulated in domain entities - ✅ Ubiquitous language evident in code (Basket, Order, Customer) - ✅ Aggregate boundaries enforce consistency - ✅ Domain events enable loose coupling - ✅ Testable business rules without database Trade-offs: - ⚠️ Requires deeper OOP understanding - ⚠️ Can be over-engineered for simple CRUD scenarios - ⚠️ Learning curve for team members unfamiliar with DDD 3. Repository Pattern Description: Clean abstraction between domain model and data access implemented through repository interfaces defined in domain layer, with NHibernate implementations in separate data access layer. Pattern Structure: // Domain layer defines contract public interface IBasketRepository { Basket FindBy ( Guid id ); IEnumerable < Basket > FindAll (); void Save ( Basket basket ); void Delete ( Basket basket ); } // Data access layer implements with NHibernate public class BasketRepository : Repository < Basket > , IBasketRepository { public Basket FindBy ( Guid id ) { return Session . Get < Basket > ( id ); } // ... other implementations } Repositories: - BasketRepository - Basket aggregate persistence - OrderRepository - Order aggregate persistence - CustomerRepository - Customer aggregate persistence - ProductRepository - Product entity persistence - CategoryRepository - Category entity persistence - DeliveryOptionRepository - Shipping options persistence Generic Base: Repository<T> provides common CRUD operations Benefits: - ✅ Domain model independent of ORM choice - ✅ Easy to unit test (mock repositories) - ✅ Single place to optimize queries - ✅ Can switch ORM without changing domain Trade-offs: - ⚠️ Additional abstraction layer - ⚠️ Query capabilities limited by abstraction 4. Unit of Work Pattern Description: Transaction management centralized in IUnitOfWork implementation wrapping NHibernate session lifecycle. Ensures all repository operations within single request participate in same transaction. Implementation: public interface IUnitOfWork { ISession GetSession (); void Commit (); void Rollback (); } public class NHUnitOfWork : IUnitOfWork { private readonly ISession _session ; public void Commit () { using ( var transaction = _session . BeginTransaction ()) { transaction . Commit (); } } } Scope: Per HTTP request (session stored in HttpContext) Benefits: - ✅ Consistent transaction management - ✅ Automatic rollback on errors - ✅ Single database round-trip for multiple operations - ✅ Clear transaction boundaries Trade-offs: - ⚠️ Must remember to call Commit() - ⚠️ Long-running requests hold transactions 5. Service Layer Pattern Description: Business logic orchestration through service layer with request/response messaging contracts. Services coordinate between controllers, domain, and repositories. Services: - IProductCatalogService - Product catalog operations - IBasketService - Shopping basket management - IOrderService - Order processing - ICustomerService - Customer management Request/Response Pattern: // Every service method follows this pattern public SubmitOrderResponse SubmitOrder ( SubmitOrderRequest request ) { // 1. Retrieve data from repositories // 2. Execute domain logic // 3. Persist changes // 4. Commit transaction // 5. Return response } Benefits: - ✅ Clear API contracts - ✅ Transaction boundaries at service level - ✅ Testable without HTTP context - ✅ Future-ready for API extraction Trade-offs: - ⚠️ Can become anemic if too much logic moves to services - ⚠️ Request/response objects add boilerplate 6. Dependency Injection (Inversion of Control) Description: Application-wide dependency injection using StructureMap 2.5 container configured in BootStrapper class. All dependencies resolved through constructor injection. IoC Registration: // StructureMap configuration in BootStrapper.cs ForRequestedType < IProductCatalogService > () . TheDefaultIsConcreteType < ProductCatalogService > (); ForRequestedType < IBasketRepository > () . TheDefaultIsConcreteType < BasketRepository > (); ForRequestedType < IUnitOfWork > () . TheDefaultIsConcreteType < NHUnitOfWork > () . CacheBy ( InstanceScope . HttpContext ); Lifecycle Management: - Transient - New instance per resolution (default for services) - HttpContext - Singleton per HTTP request (Unit of Work, Repositories) - Singleton - Application lifetime (Configuration, Logger factory) Benefits: - ✅ Loose coupling between layers - ✅ Easy to swap implementations - ✅ Unit testing with mocks - ✅ Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit Trade-offs: - ⚠️ StructureMap 2.5 is outdated (now sunsetted) - ⚠️ Container configuration can become complex 7. State Pattern Description: Order state management implemented using State pattern to handle order lifecycle transitions (Open → Submitted). Implementation: public interface IOrderState { void Submit ( Order order ); bool CanEdit { get ; } } public class OpenOrderState : IOrderState { public void Submit ( Order order ) { // Transition to submitted state order . State = new SubmittedOrderState (); DomainEvents . Raise ( new OrderSubmittedEvent ( order )); } public bool CanEdit => true ; } public class SubmittedOrderState : IOrderState { public void Submit ( Order order ) { throw new DomainException ( "Order already submitted" ); } public bool CanEdit => false ; } Benefits: - ✅ State-specific behavior encapsulated - ✅ Clear state transitions - ✅ Extensible (easy to add new states) Trade-offs: - ⚠️ Only two states (could use simple flag) - ⚠️ State classes add complexity 8. Factory Pattern Description: Multiple factory implementations for complex object creation and proper initialization. Factories: - BasketItemFactory.Create(product, quantity) - Creates basket items - OrderItemFactory.CreateFromBasketItem(basketItem) - Converts basket items to order items - PaymentFactory.Create(paymentData) - Creates payment objects - ApplicationSettingsFactory - Loads configuration - LoggingFactory - Creates logger instances Benefits: - ✅ Centralized object creation logic - ✅ Consistent initialization - ✅ Testability (can mock factories) 9. Domain Events Pattern Description: Event-driven communication within domain using static DomainEvents class for publish-subscribe pattern. Implementation: // Domain entity raises event public class Order { public void Submit () { State . Submit ( this ); DomainEvents . Raise ( new OrderSubmittedEvent ( this )); } } // Handler registered in service layer public class OrderSubmittedHandler : IDomainEventHandler < OrderSubmittedEvent > { public void Handle ( OrderSubmittedEvent @event ) { _emailService . SendOrderConfirmation ( @event . Order ); } } Benefits: - ✅ Loose coupling between domain and infrastructure - ✅ Easy to add new event handlers - ✅ Domain stays pure (no infrastructure dependencies) Trade-offs: - ⚠️ Static class (can complicate testing) - ⚠️ Only in-process events (not distributed) Architectural Characteristics Quality Attributes Analysis Attribute Rating Analysis Evidence Performance ⚠️ Medium Adequate for OfType < Action < T >> ()) { handler ( domainEvent ); } } } // Usage in domain entity public class Order { public void Submit () { // ... business logic ... DomainEvents . docs.text: Agathas.Storefront is a classic ASP.NET MVC 2 e-commerce web application built on .NET Framework 3.5/4.0, representing a well-architected monolithic system following Domain-Driven Design principles and layered architecture patterns. The system was designed and implemented circa 2010, demonstrating mature software engineering practices for that era. The application implements a complete online storefront with product catalog browsing, shopping basket functionality, customer account management, order processing, and payment integration with PayPal. The architecture exhibits excellent separation of concerns through a 5-layer structure: Presentation (ASP.NET MVC), Business Logic (Services), Domain Model, Data Access (NHibernate), and Infrastructure (cross-cutting concerns). Despite being built with now-legacy technologies, the codebase demonstrates high-quality architectural patterns including Repository pattern, Unit of Work, Dependency Injection (StructureMap), Domain Events, Factory pattern, and State pattern. The strong architectural foundation provides a solid base for modernization efforts, though significant technology upgrades are required to address obsolescence and security concerns. Technology Stack Summary: - Platform: .NET Framework 3.5 / 4.0 - Language: C# 3.5 / 4.0 - Architecture Style: Layered Architecture with Domain-Driven Design (N-Tier Monolith) - Database: SQL Server Express LocalDB (User Instance mode) - ORM: NHibernate 2.1 with HBM.XML mappings - Client Technology: ASP.NET MVC 2, ASPX Views, jQuery 1.3.2 - Integration: HTTP POST (PayPal), OAuth-style callback (Janrain), SMTP (Email) - Dependency Injection: StructureMap 2.5

docs.text: Communication Patterns: - Synchronous: All communication is synchronous method calls within the monolithic process - Asynchronous: None - no message queues or async processing - Event-Driven: Domain Events within same process (not distributed events) Protocols Used: - Internal: Direct method calls via dependency injection - External HTTP/HTTPS: PayPal (Form POST), Janrain (OAuth callback), SMTP - Database: ADO.NET via NHibernate ORM (SQL protocol) Dependency Flow: - Presentation → Business Services → Domain → Data Access → Infrastructure - Unidirectional dependencies (no circular references) - Infrastructure layer has no dependencies on application layers Hosting and Deployment: - Environment: On-premises IIS or development IIS Express - Deployment Model: Single monolithic deployment (XCOPY or Web Deploy) - Orchestration: None - traditional web application hosting - Load Balancing: Requires external load balancer (not implemented in application) - Session Affinity: Required if session state used (current implementation uses cookies)

docs.text: Typical Request Flow (Add Item to Basket Example): Request Entry - HTTP POST request arrives at BasketController.Add(productId) Authentication - [Authorize] attribute verifies Forms Authentication cookie Model Binding - MVC model binder creates AddItemToBasketRequest from form/query parameters Validation - Model validation attributes checked (e.g., [Required] , [Range] ) Service Invocation - Controller calls IBasketService.AddItemToBasket(request) Data Retrieval - Service fetches Basket and Product entities via repositories Business Logic - Domain entity Basket.AddItem() method enforces business rules Persistence - Repository saves changes through NHibernate session Transaction Commit - Unit of Work commits transaction to database Response - Controller returns redirect to basket view Error Handling Strategy: Validation Errors - Caught by MVC model validation, returns 400 Bad Request or re-displays form with errors Business Rule Violations - Domain entities throw DomainException , caught by controller, displayed as user-friendly message Data Access Errors - NHibernate exceptions caught by service layer, logged via Log4Net, returns 500 Internal Server Error External Service Failures - PayPal/Janrain failures caught, logged, display error page to user Unhandled Exceptions - Global exception filter in Global.asax logs and displays generic error page Error Response Format: - Web Requests - HTML error pages or model validation errors displayed in form - AJAX Requests - JSON responses with { success: false, message: "Error description" } Logging Strategy: - Info - Successful operations (order submitted, user registered) - Warning - Recoverable errors (validation failures, external service timeouts) - Error - Exceptions requiring attention (database errors, integration failures) - Debug - Detailed execution flow (enabled in development only) - Log Location - File system at C:\logs\ via Log4Net RollingFileAppender Transaction Management: Scope - One NHibernate session per HTTP request Isolation Level - Read Committed (SQL Server default) Commit Strategy - Explicit UnitOfWork.Commit() called by service layer after successful business logic execution Rollback Strategy - Automatic rollback on exception (session disposed without commit) Long-Running Transactions - Not used; transactions are short-lived within single HTTP request Distributed Transactions - Not implemented (single database) Request/Response Messaging Pattern: All service layer operations follow consistent request/response pattern: // Request object with parameters public class AddItemToBasketRequest { public Guid BasketId { get ; set ; } public int ProductId { get ; set ; } public int Quantity { get ; set ; } } // Response object with result data and success indicator public class AddItemToBasketResponse { public bool Success { get ; set ; } public string Message { get ; set ; } public BasketView Basket { get ; set ; } } // Service interface public interface IBasketService { AddItemToBasketResponse AddItemToBasket ( AddItemToBasketRequest request ); } This pattern provides: - Clear service contracts - Testability (easy to mock request/response) - Consistency across all business operations - Future-proofing for API extraction
docs.title: Code Flow Description

docs.text: Description: The application follows a classic 5-layer architecture with strict unidirectional dependencies flowing downward: Presentation → Business Services → Domain → Data Access → Infrastructure. Each layer has clearly defined responsibilities and communicates only with adjacent layers (except Infrastructure, which is referenced by all). Structure: ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Presentation Layer (MVC Web + Controllers) │ │ - ASP.NET MVC 2 Web Application │ │ - Controllers (HTTP request handling) │ │ - View Models │ │ - Views (ASPX templates) │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ↓ depends on ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Business Services Layer │ │ - Business workflow orchestration │ │ - Request/Response messaging │ │ - Domain event handlers │ │ - Entity to ViewModel mapping │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ↓ depends on ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Domain Model Layer (DDD) │ │ - Entities and Aggregates │ │ - Business rules and invariants │ │ - Domain events │ │ - Repository interfaces │ │ - Value objects │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ↓ depends on ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Data Access Layer (NHibernate) │ │ - Repository implementations │ │ - ORM mappings (HBM.XML) │ │ - Unit of Work implementation │ │ - Query translation │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ ↓ uses ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Infrastructure Layer (Cross-Cutting Concerns) │ │ - Authentication & Authorization │ │ - Logging (Log4Net) │ │ - Configuration │ │ - Email, Payments │ │ - Domain base classes │ │ - Repository & Unit of Work abstractions │ └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ Characteristics: - Each layer is implemented as separate Visual Studio project - Dependencies are explicit via project references - No circular dependencies detected - Infrastructure layer provides foundation abstractions (no upward dependencies) Benefits: - ✅ Excellent separation of concerns - ✅ Easy to understand for new developers - ✅ Testable (can mock dependencies between layers) - ✅ Maintainable (changes localized to specific layers) - ✅ Independent layer evolution possible Trade-offs: - ⚠️ All requests pass through all layers (potential performance overhead) - ⚠️ Can lead to anemic domain model if business logic leaks to services - ⚠️ Tight coupling within monolith (difficult to extract microservices)
docs.title: 1. Layered Architecture (N-Tier)

docs.text: Description: The application demonstrates strong DDD tactical patterns implementation with well-defined aggregates, entities, value objects, domain events, repositories, and domain services. Business logic is encapsulated within the domain model rather than scattered across services. DDD Building Blocks Implemented: Aggregate Roots: - Basket - Shopping basket aggregate root - Order - Order aggregate root - Customer - Customer aggregate root - ProductTitle - Product catalog aggregate root Entities: - BasketItem , OrderItem , Product , DeliveryAddress , Payment Value Objects: - Address - Immutable address value object - Money-related values (embedded in entities) Domain Events: - OrderSubmittedEvent - Raised when order is submitted, triggers email notification Repositories (Interfaces in Domain): - IBasketRepository , IOrderRepository , ICustomerRepository , IProductRepository Domain Services: - ShippingService - Calculates shipping costs based on delivery options Factories: - BasketItemFactory - Creates basket items with proper initialization - OrderItemFactory - Creates order items from basket items - PaymentFactory - Creates payment objects Specifications: - EmailValidationSpecification - Validates email format Example Domain Logic: // Domain entity encapsulates business rules public class Basket : AggregateRoot { public void AddItem ( Product product , int quantity ) { // Business rule: quantity must be positive if ( quantity <= 0 ) throw new DomainException ( "Quantity must be greater than zero" ); // Business rule: check if item already exists var existingItem = Items . FirstOrDefault ( i => i . ProductId == product . Id ); if ( existingItem != null ) { existingItem . IncreaseQuantity ( quantity ); } else { Items . Add ( BasketItemFactory . Create ( product , quantity )); } // Aggregate maintains own consistency RecalculateTotal (); } } Benefits: - ✅ Business logic clearly encapsulated in domain entities - ✅ Ubiquitous language evident in code (Basket, Order, Customer) - ✅ Aggregate boundaries enforce consistency - ✅ Domain events enable loose coupling - ✅ Testable business rules without database Trade-offs: - ⚠️ Requires deeper OOP understanding - ⚠️ Can be over-engineered for simple CRUD scenarios - ⚠️ Learning curve for team members unfamiliar with DDD
docs.title: 2. Domain-Driven Design (DDD)

docs.text: Description: Clean abstraction between domain model and data access implemented through repository interfaces defined in domain layer, with NHibernate implementations in separate data access layer. Pattern Structure: // Domain layer defines contract public interface IBasketRepository { Basket FindBy ( Guid id ); IEnumerable < Basket > FindAll (); void Save ( Basket basket ); void Delete ( Basket basket ); } // Data access layer implements with NHibernate public class BasketRepository : Repository < Basket > , IBasketRepository { public Basket FindBy ( Guid id ) { return Session . Get < Basket > ( id ); } // ... other implementations } Repositories: - BasketRepository - Basket aggregate persistence - OrderRepository - Order aggregate persistence - CustomerRepository - Customer aggregate persistence - ProductRepository - Product entity persistence - CategoryRepository - Category entity persistence - DeliveryOptionRepository - Shipping options persistence Generic Base: Repository<T> provides common CRUD operations Benefits: - ✅ Domain model independent of ORM choice - ✅ Easy to unit test (mock repositories) - ✅ Single place to optimize queries - ✅ Can switch ORM without changing domain Trade-offs: - ⚠️ Additional abstraction layer - ⚠️ Query capabilities limited by abstraction
docs.title: 3. Repository Pattern

docs.text: Description: Transaction management centralized in IUnitOfWork implementation wrapping NHibernate session lifecycle. Ensures all repository operations within single request participate in same transaction. Implementation: public interface IUnitOfWork { ISession GetSession (); void Commit (); void Rollback (); } public class NHUnitOfWork : IUnitOfWork { private readonly ISession _session ; public void Commit () { using ( var transaction = _session . BeginTransaction ()) { transaction . Commit (); } } } Scope: Per HTTP request (session stored in HttpContext) Benefits: - ✅ Consistent transaction management - ✅ Automatic rollback on errors - ✅ Single database round-trip for multiple operations - ✅ Clear transaction boundaries Trade-offs: - ⚠️ Must remember to call Commit() - ⚠️ Long-running requests hold transactions
docs.title: 4. Unit of Work Pattern

docs.text: Description: Business logic orchestration through service layer with request/response messaging contracts. Services coordinate between controllers, domain, and repositories. Services: - IProductCatalogService - Product catalog operations - IBasketService - Shopping basket management - IOrderService - Order processing - ICustomerService - Customer management Request/Response Pattern: // Every service method follows this pattern public SubmitOrderResponse SubmitOrder ( SubmitOrderRequest request ) { // 1. Retrieve data from repositories // 2. Execute domain logic // 3. Persist changes // 4. Commit transaction // 5. Return response } Benefits: - ✅ Clear API contracts - ✅ Transaction boundaries at service level - ✅ Testable without HTTP context - ✅ Future-ready for API extraction Trade-offs: - ⚠️ Can become anemic if too much logic moves to services - ⚠️ Request/response objects add boilerplate
docs.title: 5. Service Layer Pattern

docs.text: Description: Application-wide dependency injection using StructureMap 2.5 container configured in BootStrapper class. All dependencies resolved through constructor injection. IoC Registration: // StructureMap configuration in BootStrapper.cs ForRequestedType < IProductCatalogService > () . TheDefaultIsConcreteType < ProductCatalogService > (); ForRequestedType < IBasketRepository > () . TheDefaultIsConcreteType < BasketRepository > (); ForRequestedType < IUnitOfWork > () . TheDefaultIsConcreteType < NHUnitOfWork > () . CacheBy ( InstanceScope . HttpContext ); Lifecycle Management: - Transient - New instance per resolution (default for services) - HttpContext - Singleton per HTTP request (Unit of Work, Repositories) - Singleton - Application lifetime (Configuration, Logger factory) Benefits: - ✅ Loose coupling between layers - ✅ Easy to swap implementations - ✅ Unit testing with mocks - ✅ Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit Trade-offs: - ⚠️ StructureMap 2.5 is outdated (now sunsetted) - ⚠️ Container configuration can become complex
docs.title: 6. Dependency Injection (Inversion of Control)

docs.text: Description: Order state management implemented using State pattern to handle order lifecycle transitions (Open → Submitted). Implementation: public interface IOrderState { void Submit ( Order order ); bool CanEdit { get ; } } public class OpenOrderState : IOrderState { public void Submit ( Order order ) { // Transition to submitted state order . State = new SubmittedOrderState (); DomainEvents . Raise ( new OrderSubmittedEvent ( order )); } public bool CanEdit => true ; } public class SubmittedOrderState : IOrderState { public void Submit ( Order order ) { throw new DomainException ( "Order already submitted" ); } public bool CanEdit => false ; } Benefits: - ✅ State-specific behavior encapsulated - ✅ Clear state transitions - ✅ Extensible (easy to add new states) Trade-offs: - ⚠️ Only two states (could use simple flag) - ⚠️ State classes add complexity
docs.title: 7. State Pattern

docs.text: Description: Multiple factory implementations for complex object creation and proper initialization. Factories: - BasketItemFactory.Create(product, quantity) - Creates basket items - OrderItemFactory.CreateFromBasketItem(basketItem) - Converts basket items to order items - PaymentFactory.Create(paymentData) - Creates payment objects - ApplicationSettingsFactory - Loads configuration - LoggingFactory - Creates logger instances Benefits: - ✅ Centralized object creation logic - ✅ Consistent initialization - ✅ Testability (can mock factories)
docs.title: 8. Factory Pattern

docs.text: Description: Event-driven communication within domain using static DomainEvents class for publish-subscribe pattern. Implementation: // Domain entity raises event public class Order { public void Submit () { State . Submit ( this ); DomainEvents . Raise ( new OrderSubmittedEvent ( this )); } } // Handler registered in service layer public class OrderSubmittedHandler : IDomainEventHandler < OrderSubmittedEvent > { public void Handle ( OrderSubmittedEvent @event ) { _emailService . SendOrderConfirmation ( @event . Order ); } } Benefits: - ✅ Loose coupling between domain and infrastructure - ✅ Easy to add new event handlers - ✅ Domain stays pure (no infrastructure dependencies) Trade-offs: - ⚠️ Static class (can complicate testing) - ⚠️ Only in-process events (not distributed)
docs.title: 9. Domain Events Pattern

docs.text: Attribute Rating Analysis Evidence Performance ⚠️ Medium Adequate for small-scale e-commerce; no caching implemented (caching layer exists but disabled); N+1 query potential with lazy loading; synchronous processing only NHibernate lazy loading enabled; No caching configuration active; Single-threaded request processing Scalability ❌ Low Monolithic architecture with session affinity required; SQL Server User Instance not production-ready; In-memory session state limits horizontal scaling; No load balancing implementation User Instance database mode; HttpContext-scoped Unit of Work; No distributed caching Availability ❌ Low Single point of failure (monolith); No redundancy or failover; LocalDB not suitable for production; No health checks Single instance deployment; LocalDB architecture; No monitoring Reliability ✅ Medium Good error handling in business logic; Transaction management via Unit of Work; Domain events for decoupling; Explicit transaction commits reduce risk of partial updates Explicit UnitOfWork.Commit() pattern; Try-catch blocks in controllers; Domain exceptions Maintainability ✅ High Excellent layered architecture; Clear separation of concerns; DDD patterns well implemented; SOLID principles followed; Good naming conventions 5-layer architecture; Interface-based abstractions; Dependency injection throughout Security ❌ Critical Outdated frameworks with known vulnerabilities (jQuery 1.3.2, ASP.NET MVC 2, .NET 3.5/4.0); Plaintext secrets in Web.config; No HTTPS enforcement; No Content Security Policy; Vulnerable to modern attacks Web.config stores API keys plaintext; No RequireHttpsAttribute; Ancient jQuery version Testability ✅ High Interface-based design; Dependency injection; Request/response pattern; Domain logic in entities testable without infrastructure All dependencies injected; Repository abstractions; No static dependencies (except DomainEvents) Portability ❌ Low Tightly coupled to Windows/.NET Framework; IIS dependency; SQL Server specific; User Instance feature deprecated; No containerization .NET Framework 3.5/4.0 (Windows only); IIS hosting; SQL Server User Instance Observability ⚠️ Low Basic logging via Log4Net; No application monitoring; No performance metrics; No distributed tracing; Logs only to file system Log4Net file appender; No APM integration; No structured logging Deployability ⚠️ Medium Traditional XCOPY or Web Deploy; No CI/CD; Manual database updates; No blue-green deployment; Configuration in Web.config requires redeployment Manual deployment process; Web.config transformations; No automation
docs.title: Quality Attributes Analysis

docs.text: Current State: - Response Time: Unknown (no benchmarking data available from static analysis) - Throughput: Single-threaded request processing; limited by synchronous operations - Resource Utilization: NHibernate session per request; connection pooling via ADO.NET - Caching: Designed but not implemented - CachedProductCatalogService decorator exists but not registered in IoC Strengths: - Repository pattern allows query optimization - Lazy loading reduces initial data transfer - Transaction scope limited to single HTTP request Concerns: - No output caching for product catalog pages - No distributed caching (all data fetched from database per request) - Lazy loading can cause N+1 query problem - Synchronous PayPal redirect blocks request thread - No asynchronous processing for long-running operations Optimization Opportunities: - Enable CachedProductCatalogService decorator for read-heavy catalog operations - Implement output caching for static product pages - Add distributed cache (Redis/Memcached) for basket and session data - Optimize NHibernate queries with eager loading where appropriate - Add database query result caching
docs.title: Performance

docs.text: Horizontal Scaling: - Capability: Limited - requires session affinity due to HttpContext storage - Limitations: - Unit of Work scoped to HttpContext - SQL Server User Instance cannot be shared across servers - No distributed session management - File-based logging not suitable for multi-server Vertical Scaling: - Capability: Moderate - can add CPU/RAM to single server - Limitations: - Single-threaded request processing - LocalDB performance ceiling Bottlenecks: - SQL Server User Instance (not designed for production load) - Synchronous processing (no async/await) - NHibernate session per request (connection pool exhaustion risk) - File system logging (I/O bottleneck)
docs.title: Scalability

docs.text: Authentication: - Mechanism: ASP.NET Forms Authentication + ASP.NET Membership Provider - Strengths: Passwords hashed by Membership Provider; supports multiple auth providers - Weaknesses: - Ancient frameworks with known vulnerabilities - Password hash algorithm (SHA1) considered weak by modern standards - No multi-factor authentication - No account lockout after failed attempts visible in code - Janrain API key stored in plaintext in Web.config Authorization: - Model: Attribute-based ( [Authorize] on controllers) - Strengths: Simple and declarative - Weaknesses: - No role-based access control (RBAC) implemented - No claims-based authorization - Coarse-grained (controller level only) - No resource-based authorization Data Protection: - Encryption at Rest: None - database files unencrypted - Encryption in Transit: Depends on IIS HTTPS configuration (not enforced in code) - PII Handling: Customer data stored unencrypted - Secrets Management: Plaintext in Web.config (PayPal credentials, Janrain API key, SMTP password, connection strings) Security Controls: - Input Validation: MVC model validation attributes used - Output Encoding: ASPX views with automatic encoding (but can be bypassed) - SQL Injection Prevention: NHibernate parameterized queries provide protection - XSS Prevention: Partial - ASPX encoding helps but jQuery 1.3.2 has XSS vulnerabilities - CSRF Protection: No Anti-Forgery tokens detected Critical Vulnerabilities: - jQuery 1.3.2 has multiple known CVEs (XSS, CSRF, prototype pollution) - ASP.NET MVC 2 no longer supported, known vulnerabilities - .NET Framework 3.5/4.0 only receive critical security updates - No Content Security Policy (CSP) - No HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) - Secrets in plaintext configuration files
docs.title: Security

docs.title: Infrastructure & DevOps

docs.text: Decision: Build application on .NET Framework 3.5/4.0 with ASP.NET MVC 2 Context (circa 2010): - .NET Framework 3.5/4.0 and ASP.NET MVC 2 were modern, production-ready technologies - MVC pattern provided better separation of concerns than WebForms - Strong tooling support in Visual Studio 2010 - Rich ecosystem of libraries and community support - Enterprise-ready platform with Microsoft support Rationale: - ASP.NET MVC 2 offered testable, maintainable web development model - Mature .NET platform with extensive libraries - Good performance characteristics for web applications - Strong integration with IIS web server - Clear separation of concerns (MVC pattern) Alternatives Considered: - ASP.NET WebForms - Rejected due to tight coupling, difficult testing, ViewState overhead - Java/Spring MVC - Rejected to leverage team's .NET expertise - Ruby on Rails - Rejected due to enterprise support concerns Consequences: - ✅ Clean MVC architecture achieved - ✅ Good developer productivity with Visual Studio tooling - ✅ Strong type safety with C# - ❌ Now severely outdated (16 years old as of 2026) - ❌ Security vulnerabilities in aged framework - ❌ No longer receiving non-security updates - ❌ Talent pool shifting to .NET Core/.NET 6+ Current Status: REQUIRES MODERNIZATION - Framework obsolescence is critical technical debt
docs.title: ADR-001: Selection of .NET Framework and ASP.NET MVC

docs.text: Decision: Use NHibernate 2.1 with HBM.XML mappings for data access Context: - Need for OR/M to abstract database access - Domain-Driven Design patterns require persistence ignorance - Repository pattern implementation needs ORM support Rationale: - NHibernate was mature, proven ORM in .NET ecosystem (circa 2010) - HBM.XML mappings provide external configuration (no attributes on domain entities) - Excellent lazy loading and caching capabilities - Supports complex queries via Criteria API - Unit of Work pattern aligns well with NHibernate ISession - Keeps domain model clean (no data access attributes) Alternatives Considered: - Entity Framework 1.0 - Rejected due to immaturity (EF 1.0 had significant limitations) - LINQ to SQL - Rejected due to limited capabilities and Microsoft's unclear commitment - ADO.NET directly - Rejected due to too much boilerplate and no lazy loading Consequences: - ✅ Clean domain model without ORM pollution - ✅ Repository pattern abstraction achieved - ✅ Lazy loading reduces database round-trips - ✅ HBM.XML mappings separates structure from code - ❌ HBM.XML verbose and error-prone (no compile-time checking) - ❌ NHibernate learning curve - ❌ Now at version 5.x (multiple versions behind) Current Status: CONSIDER MODERNIZATION - NHibernate still viable but upgrade to v5+ or migrate to Entity Framework Core recommended
docs.title: ADR-002: NHibernate as ORM

docs.text: Decision: Implement 5-layer architecture (Presentation, Services, Domain, Data Access, Infrastructure) with Domain-Driven Design patterns Context: - E-commerce domain has rich business logic and complex rules - Need for maintainable, testable architecture - Team familiar with object-oriented design patterns Rationale: - Layered architecture provides clear separation of concerns - DDD tactical patterns (Aggregates, Entities, Value Objects, Repositories) model complex domain effectively - Domain layer can evolve independently of infrastructure - Testability improved through dependency inversion - Each layer has single responsibility Alternatives Considered: - Transaction Script - Rejected due to business logic complexity - 3-Tier Architecture - Rejected as insufficient separation (business logic mixed with data access) - Microservices - Rejected as overengineering for initial implementation Consequences: - ✅ Excellent code organization and maintainability - ✅ Business logic clearly encapsulated in domain entities - ✅ Easy to unit test domain logic - ✅ Scalable architecture for future features - ✅ Clear boundaries between layers - ⚠️ More complex than simple CRUD architecture - ⚠️ Monolithic deployment (all layers in one process) Current Status: ACTIVE AND SOUND - Architecture is well-designed; provides good foundation for modernization
docs.title: ADR-003: Layered Architecture with DDD

docs.text: Decision: Use StructureMap 2.5 as IoC container for dependency injection Context (circa 2010): - Need for loose coupling between layers - Repository pattern requires interface-based abstractions - Constructor injection preferred over service locator Rationale: - StructureMap was leading IoC container in .NET ecosystem at the time - Convention-based registration reduces configuration code - Supports lifecycle management (singleton, per-request, transient) - Good performance characteristics - Integration with ASP.NET MVC via custom controller factory Alternatives Considered: - Unity - Rejected due to heavier configuration - Ninject - Rejected due to performance concerns - Autofac - Less mature at the time Consequences: - ✅ Loose coupling achieved throughout application - ✅ Easy to swap implementations (useful for testing) - ✅ Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit - ❌ StructureMap project now sunset (last release 2018) - ❌ Limited support for modern .NET features Current Status: REQUIRES REPLACEMENT - Migrate to Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection (built-in .NET Core DI) or modern alternatives like Autofac
docs.title: ADR-004: StructureMap for Dependency Injection

docs.text: Decision: Implement service layer with explicit Request/Response objects for all operations Context: - Need clear service contracts - Future potential for API extraction - Testability requirements Rationale: - Request objects encapsulate all input parameters in single object - Response objects provide consistent structure for results - Easier to version and extend without breaking changes - Clear service boundaries - Facilitates future service-oriented architecture or API development - Improves testability (easy to construct request objects in tests) Alternatives Considered: - Primitive Parameters - Rejected due to parameter proliferation - Domain Entities Directly - Rejected due to tight coupling Consequences: - ✅ Clear, testable service contracts - ✅ Easy to add new parameters without breaking changes - ✅ Self-documenting API - ✅ Future-ready for API extraction - ⚠️ More boilerplate code (request/response classes) - ⚠️ Mapping overhead between requests and domain entities Current Status: ACTIVE AND SOUND - Good pattern that simplifies future API development
docs.title: ADR-005: Request/Response Messaging Pattern for Service Layer

docs.text: Decision: Use PayPal Standard Payments (redirect-based) for payment processing Context (circa 2010): - Need secure payment processing without PCI-DSS compliance burden - Credit card data must not be stored in application - Small e-commerce site without complex payment requirements Rationale: - PayPal Standard Payments offloads PCI-DSS compliance to PayPal - Simple integration via HTML form POST - No credit card data touches application servers - Widely trusted by customers - Lower transaction fees than merchant account + gateway - No monthly fees (pay-per-transaction) Alternatives Considered: - PayPal Pro - Rejected due to monthly fees and PCI requirements - Authorize.Net - Rejected due to cost and complexity - Stripe - Not available/popular in 2010 Consequences: - ✅ PCI-DSS compliance simplified (PayPal handles card data) - ✅ Easy integration (no complex API) - ✅ Customer trust in PayPal brand - ❌ Customer redirected away from site (breaks user experience) - ❌ No control over payment UI - ❌ Callback-based flow complex to test Current Status: CONSIDER MODERNIZATION - Modern embedded payment solutions (Stripe Elements, PayPal SDK) provide better UX while maintaining security
docs.title: ADR-006: PayPal Standard Payments Integration

docs.text: Status: Deprecated (Requires Immediate Remediation) Context: The application uses SQL Server Express LocalDB with User Instance mode for both main application database ( Shop.mdf ) and ASP.NET Membership database ( aspnetdb.mdf ). Files are stored in App_Data\ folder with AttachDbFilename and User Instance=true connection string parameters. Decision: Use SQL Server Express LocalDB User Instance mode for development and deployment simplicity. Original Rationale (circa 2010): - Zero-configuration database deployment - XCOPY deployment with database files - No separate SQL Server installation required - Suitable for small-scale deployments - Good for development and testing Consequences: - ✅ Positive (Original): - Simple deployment (just copy MDF files) - No DBA required for initial setup - Works out of the box for development ⚠️ Neutral/Trade-offs: File-based database limits concurrent access No central management or monitoring ❌ Negative (Current Critical Issues): User Instance feature deprecated in SQL Server 2012 and removed in 2014 Not suitable for production workloads (performance, reliability, scalability) No backup/restore capabilities for production Single point of failure (no redundancy) Connection string exposes full file path Difficult to scale horizontally No connection pooling optimization possible Cannot support multiple application instances Alternatives (Must Consider): 1. SQL Server Express (Standard Instance): Shared SQL Server instance for multi-app support 2. SQL Server Standard/Enterprise: Production-grade SQL Server for high availability 3. Azure SQL Database: Managed cloud database with auto-scaling, backup, geo-replication 4. Cloud Database Alternatives: AWS RDS, Google Cloud SQL for managed SQL Server Implementation Notes: - Current connection strings: AttachDbFilename=|DataDirectory|Shop.mdf;Integrated Security=True;User Instance=True - Database files in Agathas.Storefront.UI.Web.MVC\App_Data\ - No migration scripts (schema embedded in HBM.XML mappings) Migration Path: 1. Immediate: Switch to SQL Server Express standard instance (eliminate User Instance) 2. Short-term: Implement proper database versioning and migration scripts 3. Long-term: Migrate to managed cloud database service (Azure SQL, AWS RDS) Related ADRs: - ADR-002 (NHibernate as ORM) - Connection string changes needed - ADR-015 (Cloud Migration Strategy) - Cloud database selection
docs.title: ADR-007: SQL Server LocalDB with User Instance

docs.text: Status: Accepted (with caveats) Context: Need for decoupling between domain layer and infrastructure services (e.g., sending email when order is submitted) without creating dependencies from domain to infrastructure. Decision: Implement domain events pattern using static DomainEvents class with publish/subscribe mechanism. Rationale: - Domain entities can raise events without knowing who handles them - Infrastructure registers event handlers at application startup - Keeps domain layer clean (no infrastructure dependencies) - Simple implementation without external event bus - Events processed synchronously in same transaction Implementation: // Static domain events class public static class DomainEvents { private static List < Delegate > _handlers = new List < Delegate > (); public static void Register < T > ( Action < T > handler ) where T : IDomainEvent { _handlers . Add ( handler ); } public static void Raise < T > ( T domainEvent ) where T : IDomainEvent { foreach ( var handler in _handlers . OfType < Action < T >> ()) { handler ( domainEvent ); } } } // Usage in domain entity public class Order { public void Submit () { // ... business logic ... DomainEvents . Raise ( new OrderSubmittedEvent ( this )); } } // Handler registered in service layer DomainEvents . Register < OrderSubmittedEvent > ( e => _emailService . SendOrderConfirmation ( e . Order )); Consequences: - ✅ Positive: - Domain layer remains infrastructure-agnostic - Easy to add new event handlers without changing domain - Events processed in same transaction as domain changes - Simple implementation without external dependencies ⚠️ Neutral/Trade-offs: Static class can complicate unit testing (requires setup/teardown) No ordering guarantees for multiple handlers Synchronous processing (blocks request thread) ❌ Negative: Not suitable for distributed events or microservices No retry or error handling for failed handlers Tight coupling to single process (cannot scale event processing) Alternatives Considered: 1. MediatR Library: Not available/popular in 2010; now excellent alternative 2. Service Bus (e.g., NServiceBus): Over-engineering for in-process events 3. Observer Pattern with Interfaces: More boilerplate, similar limitations Current Status: ACCEPTABLE FOR MONOLITH - Works well for current architecture; consider MediatR during modernization Modernization Recommendation: - Migrate to MediatR for better testability and flexibility - Consider distributed event bus (Azure Service Bus, RabbitMQ) if extracting microservices
docs.title: ADR-008: Domain Events with Static Class

docs.text: Status: Superseded (by Razor in modern .NET) Context: ASP.NET MVC 2 supported both ASPX (WebForms) view engine and Spark view engine. Razor was introduced in MVC 3. Decision: Use ASPX view engine for rendering HTML views. Rationale (circa 2010): - Default view engine in ASP.NET MVC 2 - Familiar syntax for developers transitioning from WebForms - Mature and well-documented - Strong tooling support in Visual Studio Consequences: - ✅ Positive (Original): - Immediate productivity (no learning curve) - IntelliSense support in Visual Studio - Familiar <% %> syntax ❌ Negative (Current): Verbose syntax compared to Razor ( <% %> vs @ ) Difficult to test (views are compiled at runtime) No compile-time checking of view code Obsolete technology (Razor is standard since MVC 3, released 2011) Alternatives (Modern): 1. Razor View Engine: Clean syntax, compile-time checking, strong typing 2. Blazor: Component-based UI with C# (for modern rewrite) 3. SPA Framework (React/Angular/Vue): Decoupled frontend Migration Path: - Short-term: Migrate to Razor views during ASP.NET MVC upgrade - Long-term: Consider SPA architecture with API backend

docs.text: Status: Deferred (Caching designed but not enabled) Context: Product catalog is read-heavy with relatively static data. Performance optimization through caching was considered. Decision: Caching decorator CachedProductCatalogService was implemented but not activated in IoC configuration. Evidence: - File exists: Agathas.Storefront.Services.Cache/CachedProductCatalogService.cs - Decorator pattern implemented around IProductCatalogService - NOT registered in StructureMap BootStrapper (regular ProductCatalogService used instead) Why Deferred: - Insufficient production load data to determine caching strategy - Concerns about cache invalidation complexity - Product data changes infrequently (could use long cache TTL) - Premature optimization without performance problems Consequences: - ✅ Positive: - Simpler implementation (no cache invalidation logic needed) - No stale data issues - Easy to debug (no cache-related bugs) ❌ Negative: Database hit for every product catalog request Higher database load Slower response times for product browsing Increased infrastructure costs Recommendation: - Enable caching during modernization with proper strategy: - Distributed cache (Redis/Memcached) for horizontal scaling - Cache product catalog data (categories, products, brands) - Time-based expiration (e.g., 15-30 minutes) - Event-based invalidation when products updated - Output caching for static HTML pages

docs.text: Description: Application runs on .NET Framework 3.5/4.0, released 2007-2010. As of 2026, these frameworks are 16-19 years old, only receive critical security patches, lack modern language features (async/await, LINQ enhancements, records, pattern matching), and have poor cloud-native support. Impact: - Technical: Cannot use modern C# features; poor performance compared to .NET 6+; limited library ecosystem - Security: Known vulnerabilities; delayed security patches; no active development - Business: Difficult to hire developers with legacy skillset; higher maintenance costs; cloud migration blocked - Risk: Security breaches; compliance violations; inability to innovate; vendor lock-in to Windows Severity: Critical - This is existential risk to application longevity Estimated Effort: CANNOT be estimated without runtime data . Requires: - Detailed task breakdown per project/layer - Team composition analysis (skill levels with modern .NET) - Assessment of third-party dependency migration paths - Load testing data to validate performance post-migration Recommended Approach: 1. Assess application for .NET 6+ compatibility 2. Create migration backlog with detailed task estimates 3. Set up parallel .NET 6+ proof-of-concept 4. Incremental migration strategy (gradual vs. rewrite) Mitigation Strategy: 1. Assessment Phase: - Run .NET Portability Analyzer to identify breaking changes - Inventory all dependencies and check .NET 6+ compatibility - Identify Windows-specific APIs usage (if any) Migration Strategy Options: Option A - Incremental Upgrade: .NET Framework 4.0 → 4.8 → .NET 6+ (lower risk, longer timeline) Option B - Direct Migration: .NET Framework 4.0 → .NET 6+ (faster but higher risk) Option C - Parallel Rewrite: Build .NET 6+ version while maintaining legacy (highest effort) Execution Phases: Phase 1: Upgrade to .NET Framework 4.8 (maintains Windows/.NET Framework, gets latest patches) Phase 2: Migrate to ASP.NET Core MVC on .NET 6+ Phase 3: Migrate infrastructure components Phase 4: Update data access layer (NHibernate or migrate to EF Core) Phase 5: Comprehensive testing and validation Dependencies: - Must upgrade ASP.NET MVC 2 → ASP.NET Core simultaneously - Database migration (User Instance → proper SQL Server) - ASPX views → Razor views - StructureMap → Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection - jQuery upgrade for frontend compatibility Priority Justification: This blocks ALL other modernization efforts (cloud migration, containerization, microservices, modern DevOps).
docs.title: Issue 1: .NET Framework Obsolescence

docs.text: Description: Frontend uses jQuery 1.3.2 released in 2009, containing multiple known CVEs including XSS vulnerabilities, prototype pollution, and insecure regex patterns. Impact: - Security: Exploitable XSS vulnerabilities; CSRF attacks possible; potential data theft - Compliance: Fails security audits; PCI-DSS violations; OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities - Business: Reputational damage from security incidents; legal liability; customer trust erosion - Risk: Active exploitation by attackers; potential breach of customer payment data Severity: Critical - Known exploitable vulnerabilities Estimated Effort: Low (1-2 weeks) - Replace jQuery 1.3.2 with jQuery 3.x (latest stable) - Update jQuery plugins to compatible versions - Test all AJAX functionality - Verify validation still works - Browser compatibility testing Recommended Timeline: IMMEDIATE - This is urgent security fix Mitigation Strategy: <!-- Current (VULNERABLE) --> <script src= "/Scripts/jquery-1.3.2.min.js" ></script> <!-- Upgrade to (SECURE) --> <script src= "https://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.7.1.min.js" integrity= "sha256-..." crossorigin= "anonymous" ></script> Testing Required: - All AJAX operations (basket add/update, product search) - Form validation - DOM manipulation - Event handlers - Cross-browser compatibility (Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Safari) Dependencies: - jQuery Validation plugin must be upgraded to compatible version - Microsoft AJAX helpers may need replacement with modern alternatives

docs.text: Description: Application uses SQL Server Express LocalDB with deprecated User Instance feature. Database files stored in App_Data\ folder with AttachDbFilename connection string. This architecture was designed for development/small deployments but is unsuitable for production. Impact: - Reliability: Single point of failure; no redundancy; data loss risk - Performance: Limited concurrent connections; no query optimization tools; poor under load - Scalability: Cannot scale horizontally; single database file limits growth - Operations: No backup/restore automation; difficult disaster recovery; no monitoring - Security: Database file accessible via file system; no encryption at rest; audit logging limited Severity: Critical - Production deployment with this configuration is high risk Estimated Effort: Medium (2-4 weeks) Cannot estimate without: - Current database size (MB/GB) - Transaction volume (queries per second) - Backup/retention requirements - Availability SLA targets (e.g., 99.9% uptime) Mitigation Strategy: Immediate (Week 1-2): Migrate to SQL Server Express Standard Instance 1. Install SQL Server Express on server (or use existing instance) 2. Restore database from MDF file to named instance 3. Update connection string: Server=localhost\SQLEXPRESS;Database=AgathesShop;Integrated Security=True 4. Configure SQL Server Agent for automated backups 5. Test application connectivity and performance Short-Term (Month 1-2): Production-Ready SQL Server 1. Upgrade to SQL Server Standard/Enterprise edition (if budget allows) 2. Implement proper backup strategy: - Full backup daily - Transaction log backup every 15-30 minutes - Offsite backup storage 3. Configure monitoring and alerting 4. Optimize database (indexes, statistics, query plans) 5. Implement connection pooling best practices Long-Term (Month 3-6): Cloud Migration 1. Azure SQL Database: - Managed service (no server management) - Automatic backups with point-in-time restore - Built-in high availability - Geo-replication for disaster recovery - Auto-scaling capabilities AWS RDS for SQL Server: Similar managed service benefits Multi-AZ deployment for HA Automated backups and patching Dependencies: - NHibernate connection string configuration - Membership provider connection string update - Deployment process changes (no more XCOPY with MDF files)
docs.title: Issue 3: SQL Server User Instance Not Production-Ready

docs.text: Description: Web.config file contains sensitive credentials in plaintext: - PayPal business email and API credentials - Janrain API key - SMTP server username/password - Database connection strings This violates security best practices and compliance requirements (PCI-DSS, GDPR, SOC 2). Impact: - Security: Credentials exposed in source control; accessible to anyone with file system access; version control history contains secrets - Compliance: PCI-DSS violation (payment credentials); GDPR data protection requirements; audit failures - Business: Regulatory fines; failed security audits; customer data breach risk - Risk: Unauthorized access to payment gateway; email account hijacking; database breach Severity: Critical - Immediate compliance and security risk Estimated Effort: Low (1 week) Mitigation Strategy: Immediate (Day 1-2): Use ASP.NET Configuration Encryption # Encrypt connectionStrings section in Web.config aspnet_regiis -pe "connectionStrings" -app "/AgathsStorefront" -prov "DataProtectionConfigurationProvider" # Encrypt appSettings section aspnet_regiis -pe "appSettings" -app "/AgathsStorefront" -prov "DataProtectionConfigurationProvider" Short-Term (Week 1): Environment Variables // Read from environment variables instead of Web.config var paypalApiKey = Environment . GetEnvironmentVariable ( "PAYPAL_API_KEY" ); var smtpPassword = Environment . GetEnvironmentVariable ( "SMTP_PASSWORD" ); Long-Term (Modern .NET): Azure Key Vault Integration // After migration to .NET 6+ var keyVaultUrl = "https://agathas-vault.vault.azure.net/" ; var client = new SecretClient ( new Uri ( keyVaultUrl ), new DefaultAzureCredential ()); var paypalKey = await client . GetSecretAsync ( "PayPalApiKey" ); Implementation Steps: 1. Identify all secrets in Web.config 2. Choose secrets management solution (Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault) 3. Migrate secrets to secure storage 4. Update application to read from secure storage 5. Remove plaintext secrets from Web.config 6. Scrub secrets from source control history (BFG Repo-Cleaner) Dependencies: - None - can be done immediately as standalone fix
docs.title: Issue 4: Secrets in Plaintext Web.config

docs.text: Description: Application has basic file-based logging (Log4Net) but lacks modern observability: - No Application Performance Monitoring (APM) - No request tracing or correlation IDs - No real-time metrics dashboard - No alerting on errors or performance degradation - No health checks - Logs only to file system (not searchable/queryable) Impact: - Operations: Cannot detect issues proactively; slow incident response; difficult troubleshooting; blind to performance problems - Business: Extended downtime; poor user experience; revenue loss during outages; customer churn - Development: Cannot identify bottlenecks; difficult to optimize; no production insights for feature development Severity: High - Operational risk and poor incident response Estimated Effort: Medium (1-2 weeks for basic implementation) Mitigation Strategy: Phase 1 - Immediate (1-2 weeks): Structured Logging - Replace Log4Net with Serilog (supports structured logging) - Add correlation IDs to track requests across layers - Log to ELK Stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana) or cloud logging (Azure Monitor, AWS CloudWatch) - Create dashboards for error rates, response times Phase 2 - Short-term (2-4 weeks): Application Performance Monitoring - Integrate APM solution: - Azure Application Insights (for Azure deployments) - AWS X-Ray (for AWS deployments) - Datadog / New Relic (cloud-agnostic) - Track request duration, database query performance, external API calls - Set up alerting for errors, slow requests, high CPU/memory Phase 3 - Medium-term (1-2 months): Full Observability Stack - Distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry) - Custom business metrics (orders per minute, checkout funnel metrics) - Real-time dashboards for business and technical metrics - Synthetic monitoring for uptime checks - Log aggregation and search Dependencies: - Works with current architecture (no major refactoring required) - Easier to implement after .NET upgrade (async tracing support)
docs.title: Issue 5: No Monitoring or Observability

docs.text: Description: No unit test projects detected in solution. Untested codebase makes refactoring risky and slows down development velocity. Impact: - Quality: High regression risk; bugs introduced during maintenance; difficult to verify fixes - Velocity: Slow development (manual testing); fear of changing code; technical debt accumulation - Modernization: Cannot safely refactor without tests; migration risk increases Severity: Medium - Increases risk of all other changes Estimated Effort: High (ongoing - 3-6 months to achieve good coverage) Mitigation Strategy: Phase 1 - Foundation (2-4 weeks): 1. Add test projects to solution 2. Configure testing framework (xUnit / NUnit) 3. Set up mocking library (Moq / NSubstitute) 4. Write tests for critical business logic (Order submission, Basket calculations, Payment processing) Phase 2 - Service Layer Coverage (1-2 months): 1. Test all service layer methods 2. Mock repositories and external dependencies 3. Aim for 70-80% code coverage of Services layer Phase 3 - Integration Tests (1-2 months): 1. Test repository implementations (with in-memory database) 2. Test controller actions 3. Test domain event handlers Phase 4 - Automated Testing in CI/CD (Ongoing): 1. Run tests in build pipeline 2. Fail build on test failures 3. Track code coverage metrics 4. Enforce minimum coverage thresholds Recommendations: - Start with business-critical paths (order submission, payment processing) - Test-driven development for new features going forward - Characterization tests for legacy code before refactoring

docs.text: Data Architecture - Agathas.Storefront This document provides comprehensive documentation of all data storage systems, database schemas, data flow patterns, access methods, and security considerations within the system. Table of Contents Overview Data Storage Inventory Database Schema Documentation Data Flow Diagrams ORM and Data Access Patterns Data Security and Compliance Performance Considerations Backup and Recovery Data Migration and ETL Monitoring and Diagnostics Future Considerations Overview The Agathas.Storefront application utilizes a dual-database architecture with SQL Server Express LocalDB instances for both application data and ASP.NET Membership authentication. Data access is implemented through NHibernate 2.1 ORM with HBM.XML mapping files, following Repository and Unit of Work patterns for clean separation between domain and data layers. The data architecture demonstrates strong Domain-Driven Design principles with well-defined aggregates (Basket, Order, Customer, Product) and proper enforcement of aggregate boundaries. All data access flows through repository abstractions, with NHibernate providing automatic change tracking and lazy loading capabilities. Transactions are explicitly managed through the Unit of Work pattern, scoped to HTTP request boundaries for web operations. Despite the solid architectural patterns, the implementation relies on SQL Server User Instance mode with file-based databases ( AttachDbFilename ), which is deprecated and unsuitable for production. The database schema is inferred from HBM.XML mappings rather than explicit DDL scripts, making schema versioning and deployment challenging. Data Architecture Summary: - Primary Database: SQL Server Express LocalDB (User Instance mode) - Application data - Secondary Database: SQL Server Express LocalDB - ASP.NET Membership (authentication) - Data Access: NHibernate 2.1 ORM with HBM.XML mappings - Data Volume: Unknown (cannot determine from static analysis; requires production metrics) - Transaction Volume: Unknown (requires production monitoring data) Data Storage Inventory Databases Primary Database Database Name Type Version Purpose Size Location Shop SQL Server Express LocalDB (User Instance) Primary application data storage (products, orders, customers, baskets) Unknown (static analysis limitation) App_Data\Shop.mdf aspnetdb SQL Server Express LocalDB (User Instance) ASP.NET Membership Provider (user authentication) Unknown App_Data\aspnetdb.mdf Connection Details: Shop Database: Connection String: Data Source=.\SQLEXPRESS;AttachDbFilename=|DataDirectory|Shop.mdf;Integrated Security=True;User Instance=True Authentication: Windows Integrated Security User Instance: True (DEPRECATED - removed in SQL Server 2014+) Max Pool Size: 100 (default ADO.NET setting) Connection Timeout: 15 seconds (default) aspnetdb Database: Connection String: Data Source=.\SQLEXPRESS;AttachDbFilename=|DataDirectory|aspnetdb.mdf;Integrated Security=True;User Instance=True Authentication: Windows Integrated Security Purpose: ASP.NET Membership tables (aspnet_Users, aspnet_Membership, aspnet_Profile) Critical Issues: - ❌ User Instance feature deprecated in SQL Server 2012, removed in SQL Server 2014 - ❌ File-based attach mode not suitable for production (no backup automation, poor performance, no redundancy) - ❌ |DataDirectory| maps to App_Data\ folder (file system coupling) No Secondary Databases No read replicas No analytics database No data warehouse No separate reporting database File Storage Storage Type Technology Purpose Size Access Method Database Files NTFS File System SQL Server MDF/LDF files Unknown Direct file access by SQL Server User Instance Log Files NTFS File System Log4Net rolling file appender Unknown File system write via Log4Net Static Content NTFS File System CSS, JavaScript, images Small (< 10 MB estimated) IIS serves directly from Content\ and Scripts\ folders File Storage Structure: Agathas.Storefront.UI.Web.MVC/ ├── App_Data/ │ ├── Shop.mdf (Application database) │ ├── Shop_log.ldf (Transaction log) │ ├── aspnetdb.mdf (Membership database) │ └── aspnetdb_log.ldf (Membership transaction log) ├── Content/ │ ├── Site.css │ └── Images/ │ └── Structure/ (layout images) └── Scripts/ ├── jquery-1.3.2.js ├── jquery-1.3.2.min.js ├── jquery.validate.js ├── MicrosoftAjax.js └── MicrosoftMvcAjax.js External (configured): C:\logs\ (Log4Net file appender output) Caching Cache Name Technology Purpose Size TTL Strategy NHibernate First-Level Cache In-memory (per ISession) Entity caching within single Unit of Work Small (session lifetime) Session scope (disposed per request) NHibernate Second-Level Cache Not configured Cross-session entity caching N/A Not implemented Application Cache Not implemented Page/data output caching N/A None Cache Configuration: - NHibernate First-Level Cache: Automatic (built into ISession) - Eviction Policy: Session dispose (per HTTP request) - Persistence: In-memory only - Distribution: Single process (not shared across web servers) Caching Gaps: - ❌ No second-level NHibernate cache configured - ❌ No distributed cache (Redis/Memcached) for multi-server scaling - ❌ No output caching for product catalog pages - ❌ Product catalog service decorator ( CachedProductCatalogService ) exists but not registered in IoC Message Queues Not Implemented - No asynchronous messaging infrastructure ❌ No message queue (RabbitMQ, Azure Service Bus, MSMQ) ❌ All processing is synchronous within HTTP request ❌ Domain events are in-process only (not distributed) Configuration Storage Storage Type Location Purpose Access Method Web.config File system ( Agathas.Storefront.UI.Web.MVC\Web.config ) Application settings, connection strings, mail settings ConfigurationManager.AppSettings and ConfigurationManager.ConnectionStrings Plaintext Secrets Web.config (INSECURE) PayPal credentials, Janrain API key, SMTP password Direct config read No Key Vault N/A Secrets management not implemented N/A No Feature Flags N/A Feature toggles not implemented N/A Critical Security Issues: - ❌ Secrets stored in plaintext in Web.config (PCI-DSS violation) - ❌ Configuration changes require app restart - ❌ No encryption of connectionStrings section Database Schema Documentation Schema Overview The database schema is organized around Domain-Driven Design aggregates, with NHibernate HBM.XML mappings defining the structure. Schema is inferred from mappings rather than explicit DDL scripts. Naming Conventions: Convention Meaning Example PascalCase Tables Standard SQL Server naming ProductTitle , BasketItem , DeliveryAddress PascalCase Columns Property-style naming ProductId , FirstName , CreatedDate FK Suffix Foreign key columns CustomerId , OrderId , ProductTitleId No Prefixes No tbl_ or similar prefixes Customer (not tbl_Customer ) Schema Organization: - dbo schema only - No custom schemas defined - 15 core tables - Product, ProductTitle, ProductSize, ProductColor, Brand, Category, Basket, BasketItem, Order, OrderItem, Payment, Customer, DeliveryAddress, DeliveryOption, ShippingService, Courier - No views - Direct table access only - No stored procedures - All queries via NHibernate Entity Relationship Diagram Accessibility Note: This diagram shows five aggregate clusters: Product Catalog (ProductTitle, Product, Brand, Category, ProductSize, ProductColor), Shopping Basket (Basket, BasketItem), Order Processing (Order, OrderItem, Payment), Customer Management (Customer, DeliveryAddress), and Shipping (DeliveryOption, ShippingService, Courier). (e.g., "Nike Air Max Running Shoe") Product : Specific variant with size/color (e.g., "Nike Air Max, Size 10, Blue") Brand : Product manufacturer/brand Category : Product categorization (hierarchical with ParentCategoryId ) ProductSize : Reference data for sizes (S, M, L, 10, 11, etc.) ProductColor : Reference data for colors Basket Aggregate Basket : Shopping cart for customer session/account BasketItem : Individual products in basket with quantity and price snapshot Order Aggregate Order : Submitted order (aggregate root) OrderItem : Products in order (converted from BasketItem on submission) Payment : Payment details for order (one-to-one relationship) Customer Aggregate Customer : Customer account information DeliveryAddress : Multiple shipping addresses per customer Shipping Reference Data DeliveryOption : Available shipping methods with cost and estimated days ShippingService : Shipping service details Courier : Courier company providing shipping Key Relationships Explained: Product Variants ProductTitle (1) → Product (Many) Cardinality: One-to-many Description: A single product title (e.g., "Nike Air Max") has multiple variant products differentiated by size and color combinations. Basket to Order Conversion BasketItem → OrderItem (data copy on order submission) Description: When customer submits order, basket items are copied to order items, freezing product name and price at time of purchase. Customer Addresses Customer (1) → DeliveryAddress (Many) Cardinality: One-to-many Description: Customers can have multiple saved shipping addresses with one marked as default. Order Payment Order (1) → Payment (1) Cardinality: One-to-one Description: Each order has exactly one payment record (no split payments supported). Critical Design Patterns: Soft Delete : IsActive boolean columns on Product and Customer for logical deletion Price Snapshotting : OrderItem stores UnitPrice and ProductName at time of purchase (not Get < Product > ( productId ); // Safe: Criteria API uses parameters var criteria = session . CreateCriteria < Product > () . Add ( Restrictions . Eq ( "Id" , productId )); // Parameter binding // Safe: Query object pattern abstracts criteria var query = new ProductsByCategoryQuery ( categoryId ); var products = repository . FindAll ( query ); Risk Areas: - ⚠️ No evidence of raw SQL or HQL queries with string concatenation - ✅ All queries go through Repository abstraction - ✅ No stored procedures with dynamic SQL Performance Considerations Query Performance Identified Performance Risks: N+1 Query Problem: Risk: Lazy loading can trigger multiple queries Example: Loading baskets, then accessing basket.Items in loop (1 + N queries) Mitigation: Use Fetch() or eager loading in HBM.XML for known access patterns No Second-Level Caching: Impact: Every product catalog request hits database Mitigation: Enable NHibernate second-level cache (SysCache2 provider for ASP.NET cache or migrate to Redis) No Query Result Caching: Impact: Repeated identical queries (e.g., "get featured products") execute each time Mitigation: Enable NHibernate query cache Batch Size Not Optimized: Current: Batch size = 10 Recommendation: Increase to 25-50 for bulk INSERT/UPDATE operations Database Index Strategy: Cannot determine actual indexes from static analysis (requires SSMS or schema inspection). Recommended indexes based on query patterns: -- Product catalog searches (frequently queried) CREATE INDEX IX_Product_ProductTitleId ON Product ( ProductTitleId ) INCLUDE ( Price , IsActive ); CREATE INDEX IX_Product_IsActive_Price ON Product ( IsActive , Price ); CREATE INDEX IX_ProductTitle_CategoryId ON ProductTitle ( CategoryId ) INCLUDE ( Name , BrandId ); CREATE INDEX IX_ProductTitle_BrandId ON ProductTitle ( BrandId ); -- Basket operations CREATE INDEX IX_Basket_CustomerId ON Basket ( CustomerId ); CREATE INDEX IX_BasketItem_BasketId ON BasketItem ( BasketId ) INCLUDE ( ProductId , Quantity , UnitPrice ); -- Order queries CREATE INDEX IX_Order_CustomerId_OrderDate ON Order ( CustomerId , OrderDate DESC ); CREATE INDEX IX_Order_OrderNumber ON Order ( OrderNumber ); -- Unique index for order lookup CREATE INDEX IX_OrderItem_OrderId ON OrderItem ( OrderId ) INCLUDE ( ProductId , Quantity , UnitPrice ); Connection Pool Management ADO.NET Connection Pooling: Enabled by default Settings (default): - Max Pool Size: 100 - Min Pool Size: 0 - Connection Timeout: 15 seconds - Connection Lifetime: 0 (never removed from pool) NHibernate Session Management: - Scope: One ISession per HTTP request (via InstanceScope.HttpContext in StructureMap) - Risk: Long-running requests hold connections - Mitigation: Keep HTTP requests short; move long operations to background jobs Performance Monitoring Gaps Current State: - ❌ No query execution time logging - ❌ No slow query identification - ❌ No connection pool monitoring - ❌ No APM (Application Performance Monitoring) - ✅ show_sql enabled (logs all SQL) - useful for development but should be disabled in production Recommendations: 1. Integrate NHibernate with SQL Server Profiler or Extended Events for query analysis 2. Add Application Insights or similar APM tool 3. Log slow queries (> 1 second) with stack traces 4. Monitor connection pool exhaustion events Backup and Recovery Current Backup Strategy Status: ❌ No Automated Backups Detected Current State: - SQL Server User Instance mode relies on MDF file copies - No SQL Server Agent (not available in User Instance mode) - No automated backup jobs - Manual file system backups only (if implemented by operations team) Recovery Capabilities: - RPO (Recovery Point Objective): Unknown - depends on manual backup frequency - RTO (Recovery Time Objective): Unknown - no documented recovery procedure - Point-in-Time Recovery: ❌ Not possible with current architecture Critical Gaps: - No backup schedule - No backup retention policy - No offsite backup storage - No backup testing/validation - No disaster recovery plan - No high availability (single database file) Recommended Backup Strategy Immediate (Switch to SQL Server Express Standard Instance): -- Full backup (daily at 2 AM) BACKUP DATABASE AgathesShop TO DISK = 'C:\SQLBackups\AgathesShop_Full.bak' WITH INIT , FORMAT , COMPRESSION ; -- Transaction log backup (every 15 minutes) BACKUP LOG AgathesShop TO DISK = 'C:\SQLBackups\AgathesShop_Log.trn' WITH INIT , FORMAT , COMPRESSION ; SQL Server Agent Job Schedule: - Full backup: Daily at 2:00 AM - Transaction log backup: Every 15 minutes - Backup retention: 7 days local, 30 days offsite Short-Term (Production-Ready): Backup Type Frequency Retention Location Full Backup Daily (2 AM) 7 days local, 30 days cloud Local disk + Azure Blob Storage / AWS S3 Differential Backup Every 6 hours 2 days Local disk Transaction Log Backup Every 15 minutes 2 days local, 7 days cloud Local disk + cloud Backup Validation Weekly N/A Restore test to separate instance Long-Term (Cloud Migration): Azure SQL Database: Automatic backups with point-in-time restore (7-35 days retention) AWS RDS: Automatic snapshots with point-in-time recovery Geo-Replication: Active-passive replica in different region for disaster recovery Data Migration and ETL Current State No ETL Processes Detected: - ❌ No data import jobs - ❌ No data export functionality - ❌ No integration with external data sources - ❌ No data warehouse or analytics database Schema Versioning: - ❌ No database migration scripts - ❌ Schema inferred from NHibernate HBM.XML mappings - ❌ No version control for database schema - ❌ No rollback capability for schema changes Deployment Process: - Manual database creation (via HBM.XML schema export or manual script execution) - No automated schema updates during deployment Recommended Data Migration Strategy Schema Versioning Tools: Option 1: FluentMigrator (C#-based migrations) [Migration(20260609001)] public class AddProductColorTable : Migration { public override void Up () { Create . Table ( "ProductColor" ); } } Option 2: DbUp (SQL script-based migrations) Option 3: Entity Framework Core Migrations (if migrating from NHibernate to EF Core) Migration Workflow: 1. Create migration script for each schema change 2. Version migrations in source control 3. Automated deployment applies pending migrations 4. Rollback capability via Down() methods Data Seeding: - Create seed data scripts for reference data (ProductSize, ProductColor, DeliveryOption, etc.) - Idempotent scripts (can run multiple times
