docs.text: The Agathas.Storefront application utilizes a dual-database architecture with SQL Server Express LocalDB instances for both application data and ASP.NET Membership authentication. Data access is implemented through NHibernate 2.1 ORM with HBM.XML mapping files, following Repository and Unit of Work patterns for clean separation between domain and data layers. The data architecture demonstrates strong Domain-Driven Design principles with well-defined aggregates (Basket, Order, Customer, Product) and proper enforcement of aggregate boundaries. All data access flows through repository abstractions, with NHibernate providing automatic change tracking and lazy loading capabilities. Transactions are explicitly managed through the Unit of Work pattern, scoped to HTTP request boundaries for web operations. Despite the solid architectural patterns, the implementation relies on SQL Server User Instance mode with file-based databases ( AttachDbFilename ), which is deprecated and unsuitable for production. The database schema is inferred from HBM.XML mappings rather than explicit DDL scripts, making schema versioning and deployment challenging. Data Architecture Summary: - Primary Database: SQL Server Express LocalDB (User Instance mode) - Application data - Secondary Database: SQL Server Express LocalDB - ASP.NET Membership (authentication) - Data Access: NHibernate 2.1 ORM with HBM.XML mappings - Data Volume: Unknown (cannot determine from static analysis; requires production metrics) - Transaction Volume: Unknown (requires production monitoring data)

docs.text: Key Entity Groups: Product Catalog Aggregate ProductTitle : Master product record (e.g., "Nike Air Max Running Shoe") Product : Specific variant with size/color (e.g., "Nike Air Max, Size 10, Blue") Brand : Product manufacturer/brand Category : Product categorization (hierarchical with ParentCategoryId ) ProductSize : Reference data for sizes (S, M, L, 10, 11, etc.) ProductColor : Reference data for colors Basket Aggregate Basket : Shopping cart for customer session/account BasketItem : Individual products in basket with quantity and price snapshot Order Aggregate Order : Submitted order (aggregate root) OrderItem : Products in order (converted from BasketItem on submission) Payment : Payment details for order (one-to-one relationship) Customer Aggregate Customer : Customer account information DeliveryAddress : Multiple shipping addresses per customer Shipping Reference Data DeliveryOption : Available shipping methods with cost and estimated days ShippingService : Shipping service details Courier : Courier company providing shipping Key Relationships Explained: Product Variants ProductTitle (1) → Product (Many) Cardinality: One-to-many Description: A single product title (e.g., "Nike Air Max") has multiple variant products differentiated by size and color combinations. Basket to Order Conversion BasketItem → OrderItem (data copy on order submission) Description: When customer submits order, basket items are copied to order items, freezing product name and price at time of purchase. Customer Addresses Customer (1) → DeliveryAddress (Many) Cardinality: One-to-many Description: Customers can have multiple saved shipping addresses with one marked as default. Order Payment Order (1) → Payment (1) Cardinality: One-to-one Description: Each order has exactly one payment record (no split payments supported). Critical Design Patterns: Soft Delete : IsActive boolean columns on Product and Customer for logical deletion Price Snapshotting : OrderItem stores UnitPrice and ProductName at time of purchase (not foreign key to Product) Aggregate Roots : Basket, Order, Customer, ProductTitle are aggregate roots with cascading operations Audit Trail : CreatedDate, LastUpdated, OrderDate, SubmittedDate for temporal tracking Hierarchical Categories : Category table has self-referencing ParentCategoryId for tree structure

Configure (); // Read from hibernate.cfg.xml configuration . AddAssembly ( "Agathas.Storefront.Repository.NHibernate" ); _sessionFactory = configuration . BuildSessionFactory (); } return _sessionFactory ; } } // Unit of Work manages session per HTTP request public class NHUnitOfWork : IUnitOfWork { private readonly ISession _session ; public NHUnitOfWork ( ISessionFactory sessionFactory ) { _session = sessionFactory . OpenSession (); } public ISession GetSession () => _session ; public void Commit () { using ( var transaction = _session . BeginTransaction ()) { _session . Flush (); // Write pending changes transaction . Commit (); } } public void Dispose () { _session ?. Dispose (); } } Session Storage: HTTP Context (one session per web request)

docs.text: Pattern: Generic Repository with specialized interfaces Base Repository: public class Repository < T > : IRepository < T > where T : class { protected ISession Session { get ; private set ; } public Repository ( IUnitOfWork unitOfWork ) { Session = unitOfWork . GetSession (); } public T FindBy ( IQuery query ) { var criteria = query . BuildCriteria ( Session ); return criteria . UniqueResult < T > (); } public IEnumerable < T > FindAll ( IQuery query ) { var criteria = query . BuildCriteria ( Session ); return criteria . List < T > (); } public void Save ( T entity ) { Session . SaveOrUpdate ( entity ); } public void Delete ( T entity ) { Session . Delete ( entity ); } } Specialized Repository Example: public class BasketRepository : Repository < Basket > , IBasketRepository { public BasketRepository ( IUnitOfWork unitOfWork ) : base ( unitOfWork ) { } public Basket FindByCustomerId ( int customerId ) { return Session . Query < Basket > () . Where ( b => b . Customer . Id == customerId ) . Fetch ( b => b . Items ) // Eager load basket items . SingleOrDefault (); } }
docs.title: Repository Pattern Implementation

docs.text: Purpose: Abstract query construction from repository Example: public class ProductsByCategoryQuery : IQuery { private readonly int _categoryId ; public ProductsByCategoryQuery ( int categoryId ) { _categoryId = categoryId ; } public ICriteria BuildCriteria ( ISession session ) { return session . CreateCriteria < Product > () . CreateAlias ( "ProductTitle" , "pt" ) . Add ( Restrictions . Eq ( "pt.Category.Id" , _categoryId )) . Add ( Restrictions . Eq ( "IsActive" , true )) . SetMaxResults ( 50 ); } } // Usage in repository var query = new ProductsByCategoryQuery ( categoryId ); var products = repository . FindAll ( query );

docs.text: Lazy Loading Configuration: Enabled via LinFu proxies N+1 Problem Risk: // BAD: N+1 queries var baskets = basketRepository . FindAll (); foreach ( var basket in baskets ) // 1 query { Console . WriteLine ( basket . Items . Count ); // N queries (one per basket) } // GOOD: Eager loading var baskets = session . Query < Basket > () . Fetch ( b => b . Items ) // Single JOIN query . ToList (); Eager Loading Strategies: - Fetch in Query Objects for known access patterns - Join Fetch in HBM.XML for required associations - Batch fetching with batch-size attribute

docs.text: Encryption at Rest: - ❌ Database: SQL Server Express does not support Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) - feature only in Enterprise Edition - ❌ File System: No BitLocker or file-level encryption detected - ❌ Backups: No encrypted backups Encryption in Transit: - ⚠️ HTTPS: Dependent on IIS configuration (not enforced in application code) - ❌ No HSTS: HTTP Strict Transport Security not configured - ❌ No Certificate Pinning: Not applicable for web applications Recommended Encryption Strategy: Immediate: Encrypt Web.config sections: aspnet_regiis -pe "connectionStrings" -app "/AgathsStorefront" Enforce HTTPS via [RequireHttps] attribute on all controllers Short-term: Migrate secrets to Azure Key Vault or AWS Secrets Manager Implement column-level encryption for sensitive fields (use Always Encrypted if migrating to Azure SQL) Long-term: Full database encryption (TDE if using SQL Server Enterprise or Azure SQL) Implement encryption key rotation Audit logging for data access

docs.text: Protection Mechanism: NHibernate parameterized queries Risk Assessment: ✅ Low All database access flows through NHibernate ORM, which uses parameterized queries by default: // Safe: NHibernate parameterizes automatically var product = session . Get < Product > ( productId ); // Safe: Criteria API uses parameters var criteria = session . CreateCriteria < Product > () . Add ( Restrictions . Eq ( "Id" , productId )); // Parameter binding // Safe: Query object pattern abstracts criteria var query = new ProductsByCategoryQuery ( categoryId ); var products = repository . FindAll ( query ); Risk Areas: - ⚠️ No evidence of raw SQL or HQL queries with string concatenation - ✅ All queries go through Repository abstraction - ✅ No stored procedures with dynamic SQL

docs.text: Identified Performance Risks: N+1 Query Problem: Risk: Lazy loading can trigger multiple queries Example: Loading baskets, then accessing basket.Items in loop (1 + N queries) Mitigation: Use Fetch() or eager loading in HBM.XML for known access patterns No Second-Level Caching: Impact: Every product catalog request hits database Mitigation: Enable NHibernate second-level cache (SysCache2 provider for ASP.NET cache or migrate to Redis) No Query Result Caching: Impact: Repeated identical queries (e.g., "get featured products") execute each time Mitigation: Enable NHibernate query cache Batch Size Not Optimized: Current: Batch size = 10 Recommendation: Increase to 25-50 for bulk INSERT/UPDATE operations Database Index Strategy: Cannot determine actual indexes from static analysis (requires SSMS or schema inspection). Recommended indexes based on query patterns: -- Product catalog searches (frequently queried) CREATE INDEX IX_Product_ProductTitleId ON Product ( ProductTitleId ) INCLUDE ( Price , IsActive ); CREATE INDEX IX_Product_IsActive_Price ON Product ( IsActive , Price ); CREATE INDEX IX_ProductTitle_CategoryId ON ProductTitle ( CategoryId ) INCLUDE ( Name , BrandId ); CREATE INDEX IX_ProductTitle_BrandId ON ProductTitle ( BrandId ); -- Basket operations CREATE INDEX IX_Basket_CustomerId ON Basket ( CustomerId ); CREATE INDEX IX_BasketItem_BasketId ON BasketItem ( BasketId ) INCLUDE ( ProductId , Quantity , UnitPrice ); -- Order queries CREATE INDEX IX_Order_CustomerId_OrderDate ON Order ( CustomerId , OrderDate DESC ); CREATE INDEX IX_Order_OrderNumber ON Order ( OrderNumber ); -- Unique index for order lookup CREATE INDEX IX_OrderItem_OrderId ON OrderItem ( OrderId ) INCLUDE ( ProductId , Quantity , UnitPrice );

docs.text: API Integration Catalog - Agathas.Storefront This document provides a comprehensive catalog of all HTTP endpoints (MVC actions), external integration points, and integration patterns used within the system. IMPORTANT NOTE: Agathas.Storefront is an ASP.NET MVC 2 server-side web application, NOT a REST API. This document catalogs MVC controller endpoints (for web page requests) and external service integrations. The application does not expose a standalone REST API for external consumers. Table of Contents Executive Summary MVC Endpoint Catalog External API Dependencies Integration Sequence Diagrams API Security Analysis Performance Characteristics API Limitations and Constraints Monitoring and Observability Migration Recommendations Executive Summary Overview Agathas.Storefront implements a traditional server-side MVC architecture with 9 controllers and approximately 30 HTTP endpoints serving HTML pages to web browsers. The application integrates with 3 external services (PayPal for payments, Janrain for social authentication, SMTP for email) but does not expose a REST API for third-party consumption. All HTTP endpoints follow ASP.NET MVC 2 conventions with server-side rendering using ASPX views. A small number of endpoints return JSON for AJAX operations (product search, basket quantity updates). Authentication uses Forms Authentication with session cookies. The architecture is monolithic with no API gateway, no rate limiting, and no API versioning. External integrations use simple protocols (HTTP POST redirects for PayPal, OAuth callbacks for Janrain, SMTP for email). Key Statistics Metric Count Notes MVC Controllers 9 HTTP endpoints for web page requests Total Endpoints ~30 GET/POST actions serving HTML or JSON External Integrations 3 PayPal, Janrain, SMTP email Authentication Methods 2 Forms Authentication (local), Janrain (social login) API Protocols HTTP ASP.NET MVC routing, no REST/GraphQL Average Response Time Unknown No monitoring data available Daily API Calls Unknown Production metrics not available Technology Summary HTTP Technologies: - MVC Framework: ASP.NET MVC 2 (server-side rendering) - Internal Endpoints: HTTP GET/POST to MVC controllers - AJAX Endpoints: JSON responses for specific operations (product search, basket updates) - External Protocols: HTTPS Form POST (PayPal), OAuth callback (Janrain), SMTP - Authentication: ASP.NET Forms Authentication (cookie-based) - API Gateway: None - Documentation: None (no Swagger/OpenAPI) MVC Endpoint Catalog Overview The application exposes HTTP endpoints through 9 ASP.NET MVC controllers. Most endpoints return HTML views (ASPX templates) for browser rendering. A few endpoints return JSON for AJAX requests. Endpoint Structure: https://[domain]/[Controller]/[Action]?[parameters] Examples: https://agathas-storefront.com/Product/GetProductsByCategory?categoryId=5 https://agathas-storefront.com/Basket/Add?productId=123 https://agathas-storefront.com/Order/Detail/456 Routing Convention: Default ASP.NET MVC routing (controller/action/id) No API Versioning: All endpoints are unversioned (no v1, v2 prefixes) Controller Catalog 1. docs.text: Agathas.Storefront implements a traditional server-side MVC architecture with 9 controllers and approximately 30 HTTP endpoints serving HTML pages to web browsers. The application integrates with 3 external services (PayPal for payments, Janrain for social authentication, SMTP for email) but does not expose a REST API for third-party consumption. All HTTP endpoints follow ASP.NET MVC 2 conventions with server-side rendering using ASPX views. A small number of endpoints return JSON for AJAX operations (product search, basket quantity updates). Authentication uses Forms Authentication with session cookies. The architecture is monolithic with no API gateway, no rate limiting, and no API versioning. External integrations use simple protocols (HTTP POST redirects for PayPal, OAuth callbacks for Janrain, SMTP for email).

docs.text: Provider: PayPal Inc. Purpose: Credit card payment processing for customer orders Integration Type: Redirect-based payment (PayPal Standard Payments) Protocol: HTTPS Form POST Direction: Bidirectional (redirect to PayPal, callback from PayPal) Frequency: Per order submission (on-demand) Integration Flow: sequenceDiagram participant Customer participant App as Agathas.Storefront participant PayPal as PayPal Gateway Customer->>App: POST /Checkout/SubmitOrder App->>App: Create Order in database App->>PayPal: Redirect with Form POST (order details, amounts, return URL) activate PayPal PayPal->>Customer: Display payment page Customer->>PayPal: Enter payment details PayPal->>PayPal: Process payment PayPal->>App: Redirect to /Payment/Complete?orderId=X&tx=ABC123 deactivate PayPal App->>App: Update Order.Payment with transaction ID App->>Customer: Display order confirmation Hold "Alt" / "Option" to enable pan & zoom Endpoints: Operation Endpoint Method Purpose Process Payment https://www.sandbox.paypal.com/cgi-bin/webscr POST Redirect customer to PayPal for payment Payment Callback https://[app-domain]/Payment/Complete GET Receive payment completion notification Authentication: - Method: Business email configuration (no API key for Standard Payments) - Credentials Storage: Web.config <appSettings> PLAINTEXT (security issue) - Configuration: - PayPalBusinessEmail : Merchant's PayPal account email - PayPalReturnUrl : Success callback URL - PayPalCancelUrl : Cancellation callback URL Data Format: - Request: HTML form fields (application/x-www-form-urlencoded) - cmd=_xclick (single payment) - business=[merchant email] - item_name=[order description] - amount=[order total] - currency_code=USD - return=[success URL] - cancel_return=[cancel URL] Response: Query parameters on redirect tx=[transaction ID] st=[status: Completed/Pending/Failed] amt=[amount] cc=[currency code] Error Handling: - Retry Strategy: None (user-initiated retry) - Timeout: Dependent on customer action (no server-side timeout) - Circuit Breaker: Not applicable (redirect-based) - Fallback Strategy: Display error message, customer can retry checkout SLA/Uptime: - Provider SLA: 99.9% (PayPal published SLA) - Expected Availability: Very high (critical payment infrastructure) - Support Contact: PayPal Merchant Technical Support Cost Structure: - Model: Per-transaction fee - Rate: Typically 2.9% + $0.30 per transaction (merchant account specific) - Monthly Budget: Variable based on sales volume Monitoring: - ❌ No health check endpoint - ❌ No alerting on failures - ❌ No payment success rate monitoring - Recommendation: Implement PayPal IPN (Instant Payment Notification) for reliable payment confirmation Limitations: - Customer redirected away from site (UX disruption) - No control over payment UI - Callback reliability depends on customer completing redirect - Basic integration (no signature verification) - Sandbox mode configured (not production-ready) Documentation: - Location: Agathas.Storefront.Infrastructure/Payments/PaypalPaymentService.cs - PayPal Docs: https://developer.paypal.com/docs/classic/paypal-payments-standard/integration-guide/

Method: API Key - Credentials Storage: Web.config <appSettings> PLAINTEXT ( JanrainApiKey ) - Token Type: Temporary authentication token (short-lived) Data Format: - Request: Query parameters ( token=[auth-token] ) - Response: JSON user profile { "stat" : "ok" , "profile" : { "identifier" : "https://www.facebook.com/profile.php?id=123456" , "providerName" : "Facebook" , "name" : { "formatted" : "John Smith" , "givenName" : "John" , "familyName" : "Smith" }, "email" : "john.smith@example.com" , "verifiedEmail" : "john.smith@example.com" } } Error Handling: - Retry Strategy: User can retry social login - Timeout: 30 seconds for API validation call - Fallback Strategy: Display error message, user can use local registration/login SLA/Uptime: - Provider SLA: 99.9% (Janrain/Akamai SLA) - Expected Availability: High Cost Structure: - Model: Unknown (requires Janrain account details) - Typical Pricing: Per-user or subscription-based Monitoring: - ❌ No health check - ❌ No monitoring of authentication success rate - Recommendation: Log Janrain API failures, monitor authentication conversion rate Limitations: - Dependent on external service availability - User must have social media account - Privacy concerns (users may not want to link social accounts) - API key in plaintext (security risk) Documentation: - Location: Agathas.Storefront.Infrastructure/Authentication/JanrainAuthenticationService.cs - Janrain Docs: (legacy service, now Akamai Identity Cloud)

Method: SMTP username/password - Credentials Storage: Web.config PLAINTEXT (security issue) - Encryption: SSL/TLS (configurable) Error Handling: - Retry Strategy: No automatic retry - Timeout: SMTP client default (100 seconds) - Fallback Strategy: - Production: Log error, continue (email failure does not block order) - Development: TextLoggingEmailService logs email to file system SLA/Uptime: - Depends on SMTP provider (SendGrid, AWS SES, Mailgun, etc.) Cost Structure: - docs.text: Service Protocol Criticality Reliability Cost Model PayPal HTTPS POST Critical - Blocks revenue High (99.9% SLA) Per-transaction (~2.9% + $0.30) Janrain HTTPS OAuth High - Reduces friction High (99.9% SLA) Subscription/per-user SMTP Email SMTP Medium - Non-blocking Varies by provider Per-email or subscription Single Points of Failure: - ❌ PayPal: If down, customers cannot complete purchases (revenue loss) - ⚠️ Janrain: If down, social login unavailable (fallback: local registration) - ⚠️ SMTP: If down, order confirmations not sent (non-blocking, logged) Recommendations: 1. PayPal: Implement PayPal IPN for reliable payment confirmation 2. Janrain: Consider migrating to modern OAuth providers (Auth0, Azure AD B2C) 3. SMTP: Migrate to managed email service (SendGrid, AWS SES) with retry and monitoring 4. All: Move API keys/credentials to Azure Key Vault or AWS Secrets Manager

docs.text: Cannot be measured from static analysis - requires production monitoring Estimated Performance (based on architecture): Endpoint Type Estimated Response Time Factors Simple GET (cached) < 100ms If caching enabled Product listing (no cache) 200-500ms Database query + rendering Product detail page 100-300ms Single database lookup + related data Add to basket 100-200ms Database write + transaction Checkout/Order submission 500-1000ms Multiple database writes, email sending AJAX product search 300-600ms Complex query with joins Performance Bottlenecks: No Caching: Every product catalog request hits database Recommendation: Enable NHibernate second-level cache or output caching N+1 Query Problem: Lazy loading can trigger multiple queries Recommendation: Use eager loading (.Fetch()) for known access patterns Synchronous Email Sending: Order submission blocks until email sent (adds 100-500ms) Recommendation: Queue emails for background processing Database User Instance: Poor performance under load Recommendation: Migrate to standard SQL Server instance
